source_metadata.title: Healthcare Utilization and Impact of Antifungal Stewardships Within Respiratory Care Settings: A Systematic Literature Review

extraction_limitations: The @ATOM workflow is governed for primary literature, but the uploaded source is a systematic literature review. Extraction is therefore limited to review-level assertions and clearly tagged secondary summaries of selected included studies; these atoms should not substitute for extraction from the original primary studies.
The supplementary information referenced by the article was not included in the provided PDF, so the complete search strategy and supplemental reference list were not available for atomization.

The source contains an internal included-study count discrepancy: the abstract reports 28 included papers, whereas the main Results section and Figure 1 report 29. Both reported values are preserved as separate atoms rather than reconciled.

The source contains an internal disease-focus count discrepancy: the Results text states 25 of 29 articles focused on invasive fungal disease, whereas Figure 1 categorizes 27 records as invasive fungal disease and 2 as chronic respiratory disease. Both reported values are preserved.

The source contains an internal GRADE count discrepancy: Results states three studies reached moderate quality, while the Discussion states four. The table visually appears to mark three studies as Moderate; no value was silently corrected.
Several included-study summaries use terms such as significant without reporting effect sizes, confidence intervals, or p-values in the review text; no missing statistics were inferred.
Funding, conflict-of-interest, and data-availability statements were not identified in the provided 12-page PDF; no atoms were fabricated for absent disclosures.

atoms.canonical_statement: The review aimed to evaluate the current evidence for the use and impact of antifungal stewardship in chronic respiratory disease settings.
The authors conducted a systematic literature review based on PRISMA guidelines.
The review searched Medline via Ovid, Embase, and GlobalHealth for papers published from 1949 through 2020.
Eligible papers either implemented antifungal stewardship and reported outcomes or reported clinical outcomes of antifungal therapeutic drug monitoring.

The quality of included studies was assessed with GRADE categories of high, moderate, low, and very low.

atoms.canonical_statement: The review reports that rapid diagnostic approaches such as T2Candida and MALDI-TOF were associated with quicker diagnosis and reduced inappropriate antifungal use.

Integrated multidisciplinary antifungal stewardship programs were associated with reduced antifungal-attributed toxicities, including hepatotoxicity, and lower 30-day in-hospital mortality for candidemia.
Nwankwo et al. conducted an 18-month prospective cohort study of 178 inpatients and outpatients with chronic lung disease and fungal infections at a tertiary cardiopulmonary hospital.

population.label: Chronic lung disease inpatients and outpatients with fungal infections

atoms.canonical_statement: The Nwankwo antifungal stewardship intervention included a mycologist and pharmacist, weekly stewardship rounds, twice-weekly multidisciplinary meetings, and an outpatient clinic.

exposures.details: Mycologist and pharmacist; weekly stewardship rounds; multidisciplinary meeting twice weekly; outpatient clinic

atoms.canonical_statement: In the Nwankwo cohort, chronic pulmonary aspergillosis was the most common underlying fungal disease and accounted for 32% of the cohort.
The Nwankwo stewardship program delivered 285 specific recommendations.
The review reports a statistically significant increase in therapeutic azole dosing after implementation of the Nwankwo stewardship program.
The Nwankwo stewardship program was associated with a 44% reduction in monthly antifungal expenditure, with no deleterious effect on outcome reported by the review.

Browne et al. managed complex fungal lung infections through a multidisciplinary team comprising three respiratory physicians, an infectious disease specialist, a microbiologist, and two pharmacists; the team met six times over 12 months.

exposures.details: Three respiratory physicians, one infectious disease specialist, one microbiologist, and two pharmacists; six meetings in 12 months

atoms.canonical_statement: Of 32 cases discussed by the Browne multidisciplinary team, 13 were categorized as complex fungal lung infection.

population.label: Cases discussed by the Browne complex lung infection multidisciplinary team

concept.text: Cases categorized as complex fungal lung infection

atoms.canonical_statement: The review reports that therapeutic drug monitoring was implemented for the Browne complex fungal lung infection cases and that a significant reduction in development of resistance was noted.
The authors report that most included studies were observational and therefore began at low or very-low GRADE quality.
The Discussion states that four studies reached moderate-grade evidence.

population.label: Included studies in the final review

concept.text: Studies rated moderate quality by GRADE

atoms.canonical_statement: Only two included studies specifically focused on chronic lung disease patients with fungal infection, and both were classified as low-quality evidence by GRADE.
The authors identify small sample sizes and imprecision in the two respiratory-care stewardship studies as important sources of potential bias.
None of the papers in the review analyzed the effect of antifungal stewardship implementation on control of fungal sensitization.
The review states that evidence for optimal antifungal management in chronic respiratory disease is limited and that management and diagnosis vary substantially.

The authors conclude that evidence from invasive fungal disease settings supports antifungal stewardship as an implementation strategy that improves appropriate antifungal therapy and can reduce drug toxicity.
The authors state that it remains unclear whether long-term delivery of optimal antifungal therapy reduces acquisition or development of antifungal resistance.
The authors conclude that the application and evidence base for antifungal stewardship remain limited in chronic respiratory disease despite a high burden of fungal disease and antifungal resistance.
The authors call for further research to clarify factors that drive antifungal resistance and to assess the impact of antifungal stewardship in chronic respiratory disease settings.
